column2: Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India
column12: Whether alleged use of Pegasus spyware on citizens, journalists and activists breached privacy, and who should investigate when the Union gave only a general denial.
column13: Surveillance must meet legality, legitimate aim and proportionality; a bare national-security plea does not bar review, so the Court appointed its own expert committee.
column14: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

column2: Inayath Ali v. State of Telangana
column12: Whether a trial court could order DNA fingerprinting of two children in a dowry-harassment case where their paternity was not in issue.
column13: No. A DNA test intrudes on privacy and should not be ordered as a matter of course; the orders treating the children as evidence were set aside.

column2: X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Dept., GNCTD
column12: Whether an unmarried woman could be refused abortion at 20 to 24 weeks while married women were allowed it.
column13: The exclusion was unjustified; the rule covers unmarried women, and a woman's choice over her pregnancy is part of Art 21 liberty, dignity and privacy.
column14: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

column2: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v. Ajinkya Arun Firodia
column12: Whether a family court could order a DNA test of a child to help the husband in divorce proceedings.
column13: Not without a strong prima facie case; the legitimacy presumption and the child's privacy and welfare weigh against routine DNA testing.
column14: Nandlal Wasudeo Badwaik v. Lata Nandlal Badwaik (2014)

column2: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India
column12: Whether the Electoral Bond Scheme's donor anonymity, defended as informational privacy of political affiliation, could justify denying voters information.
column13: Privacy of political giving was accepted as a real interest, but total anonymity was disproportionate; the scheme was struck down.
column14: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)

column2: Frank Vitus v. Narcotics Control Bureau
column12: Whether bail can be conditioned on the accused dropping a Google Maps pin and getting an embassy assurance.
column13: A bail condition letting police track an accused's every movement violates Art 21 privacy; the pin condition and the embassy-certificate condition were deleted.
column14: Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee v. Union of India (1994)

column2: In Re: Right to Privacy of Adolescents
column12: Whether the High Court could acquit in a POCSO case and lecture adolescent girls on conduct, and what duties follow for courts and States.
column13: The remarks were unwarranted and offended adolescents' Art 21 rights; the conviction was restored and guidelines on judgment-writing and State duties were issued.

column12: Whether a man could be forced to take a DNA test to settle a paternity claim based on alleged adultery.
column13: No. Legitimacy settles paternity unless non-access is proved, and a roving inquiry into private life violates privacy and dignity.
column14: Goutam Kundu v. State of West Bengal (1993)

column12: Whether a husband's secret recordings of calls with his wife could be used as evidence in a divorce case.
column13: Yes. s 122 protects marital sanctity, not individual privacy, and does not bar evidence between spouses; privacy is not absolute here.

column11: s 112 Evidence Act; ss 53, 53A CrPC; Art 21
column12: Whether a doctor could be ordered to give a DNA sample in a cheating and harassment case where paternity was only collateral.
column13: No. A DNA order needs a direct link to the offence and a balance of interests; otherwise it is an unjustified intrusion on privacy and bodily autonomy.
column14: Goutam Kundu v. State of West Bengal (1993)

column12: Whether a man could be made to take a DNA test so his son could prove paternity in a civil suit.
column13: Yes. Privacy is not absolute; here the son's interest in settling his parentage outweighed the father's privacy, so the test was upheld.
